claims.text: The coupled tribo-corrosion response of high-entropy alloys is governed by the stability of the native passive oxide film.
Sliding mechanically disrupts the passive film.
Disruption of the passive film exposes fresh alloy surface.
Freshly exposed alloy surface corrodes more rapidly than film-covered surface.
Corrosion products modify surface chemistry and topography.
Corrosion-induced changes in surface chemistry and roughness influence friction and accelerate wear.
Film disruption, corrosion, and accelerated wear form a positive-feedback degradation loop.
The initial high-entropy alloy naturally possesses a passive oxide layer.
The native passive oxide contributes to the alloy's corrosion resistance.
The native passive oxide contributes to the alloy's mechanical performance.
Artificial stabilization of the passive film provides a controlled means to alter film integrity.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion will cause greater total degradation than a condition in which the passive film remains intact.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion will increase wear volume relative to the stated baseline.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion will increase corrosion rate relative to the stated baseline.
Stabilizing the passive film will diminish the corrosion contribution and reduce cumulative degradation.
The proposed mechanism should operate when corrosion is significant and passive-film formation kinetics are comparable to the rate of mechanical wear.
The proposed mechanism may fail in environments with very low corrosive aggressiveness.
The proposed mechanism may fail at extremely high wear rates where mechanical degradation dominates.
The relative corrosion and mechanical contributions vary with environmental conditions and material properties.
The synergistic interaction may be weaker under milder corrosive conditions.
